strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and timely problem: exploratory discovery of treatment-responsive outcomes from high-dimensional measurements in randomized trials, where scientists may not know the relevant outcome variables in advance.
The combination of foundation-model representations, sparse autoencoders, and causal testing is conceptually appealing and could inspire useful tools for hypothesis generation in scientific domains.

The semi-synthetic CelebA setup gives the authors a controllable environment with known affected concepts, and the paper includes several useful ablations, including zero-effect behavior, multiplicity variants, and AIPW versus simple mean differences.
The paper is generally readable and is explicit about important limitations such as dependence on measurement sufficiency, foundation-model representation quality, and SAE identifiability.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee is much weaker than it appears. NES consistency relies on strong assumptions that essentially encode successful disentanglement, principal-neuron dominance, bounded post-treatment stratification bias, and recovery of already discovered effects. These assumptions are neither verifiable nor empirically stress-tested, so the theorem provides limited assurance for realistic SAE representations.

The statistical validity of recursively stratifying on discovered SAE codes is not fully convincing. These codes are post-treatment variables, and although the paper discusses bounded collider/transport bias, the procedure lacks a rigorous finite-sample or selective-inference treatment for the adaptive testing and stopping rule.

The empirical evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main quantitative evidence is a semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark with only two affected factors and a ground truth defined by the best SAE neuron per label, which may favor the proposed framing and does not demonstrate robustness across realistic scientific measurement settings.

The real-world ecology experiment is intriguing but weak as validation: it uses only 44 videos, removes Bonferroni correction, returns one scientifically relevant behavior and one background artifact, and does not provide enough quantitative comparison to establish reliable unsupervised causal discovery.

Baselines are limited. The comparisons are mostly vanilla t-test/FDR/Bonferroni/top-k variants rather than stronger representation-level or multivariate alternatives, clustering/causal feature learning methods, supervised annotation-efficient approaches, permutation procedures, or stability-selection methods.

Claims such as the first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial are overstated relative to the evidence, especially because expert interpretation and prior known grooming annotations are used a posteriori and the discovered background signal reflects experimental imbalance rather than a meaningful causal outcome.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. Important implementation choices for SAE training, stratification binning, residualization, model selection, and code availability are under-specified or only sketched, and the real-world dataset accessibility is unclear.
Presentation has some polish issues, including typographical errors in the title/wordplay, occasional notation mistakes, and figures that are hard to read at conference-paper scale.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and interesting problem: exploratory discovery of unknown treatment effects from high-dimensional scientific measurements, framed around randomized trials, foundation-model representations, and sparse autoencoders.

The high-level motivation is compelling: standard hypothesis-driven causal analysis can miss unexpected effects, and a statistically disciplined way to surface candidate outcomes for expert follow-up would be useful in scientific workflows.

The paper includes a clear illustrative failure mode for naive multiple testing over entangled representation dimensions, and the proposed recursive search procedure is simple enough to understand and implement.

The authors evaluate on both a controlled semi-synthetic CelebA setting and a real ecological RCT, and provide some ablations for no-effect cases, testing choices, and AIPW versus simple associational differences.
weaknesses: The main theoretical claims rely on very strong and partly circular assumptions. In particular, the consistency theorem assumes distinct principal neurons, a principal-max condition, and a decomposition in which stratification cancels already discovered effects. These assumptions essentially encode the desired behavior and do not convincingly establish that NES will work for realistic SAE representations.

The causal validity of the recursive stratification step is under-justified. The selected SAE codes are post-treatment variables, and conditioning/stratifying on them can induce post-treatment or collider bias. The paper acknowledges this only through an assumed bounded transport error, but does not provide a convincing identification argument or practical diagnostic for when the bound holds.

The empirical evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The semi-synthetic benchmark uses only two CelebA attributes with a constructed data-generating process, and the ground-truth affected codes are defined by the same SAE representation family that the method searches over. This makes the evaluation partly circular and does not show robustness to realistic scientific outcomes, continuous effects, correlated outcomes, nuisance variation, or SAE instability.

The real-world experiment is weak evidence. The method is applied to only 44 videos, disables Bonferroni correction due to small sample size, and returns one known behavior plus a background artifact correlated with treatment. Calling the background discovery a strength is debatable; it also illustrates that the method may surface dataset artifacts rather than scientifically meaningful causal outcomes.

Baselines are limited. The comparison is mainly against vanilla t-tests, Bonferroni, FDR, and top-k selection. Stronger alternatives such as hierarchical testing, conditional/randomization tests, knockoffs or selective inference, sparse regression/group testing, representation-level two-sample tests, causal feature learning variants, and clustering-based effect discovery are missing.

The paper overstates novelty and significance relative to the evidence. The method is essentially greedy selection plus repeated conditional testing over learned features, and the experiments do not establish that this is a generally reliable approach for exploratory causal inference in science.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper says standalone code to reproduce all experiments will be released later, while many important details affecting results are underspecified, including SAE training stability, random seed variability, exact preprocessing, stopping behavior under relaxed correction, and how expert interpretations were performed.

The writing is sometimes imprecise and contains technical and presentation issues, such as typos in the title and text, inconsistent notation and dimensions for SAE variables, and claims like FM sufficiency or linear concept recovery that are central but not empirically validated.

strengths: Timely and interesting problem formulation: the paper clearly motivates exploratory causal inference for RCTs with high-dimensional unstructured outcomes, and the rationalist/empiricist distinction is a useful framing for scientific discovery workflows.

The proposed Neural Effect Search procedure addresses a real failure mode of naive multiple testing over entangled representation dimensions: increasing statistical power can make many semantically irrelevant leakage features significant.

The combination of foundation model features, sparse autoencoders, and causal hypothesis testing is novel and potentially impactful, especially for scientific domains where manual outcome annotation is expensive.

The semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark is thoughtfully designed to provide known treatment effects while retaining real image structure, and the reported results support the central claim that recursive adjustment improves precision/IoU over standard t-test, FDR, Bonferroni, and top-k selection.
The paper includes useful ablations, including no-effect behavior, alternative multiple-testing gates, and AIPW versus simple mean differences, which strengthens the empirical story.

The real-world ecology case study is compelling as a demonstration: recovering a known grooming-related signal without supervised labels is a meaningful proof of concept, and identifying a background artifact is a plausible example of the method surfacing experimental bias.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees rely on very strong assumptions, especially FM sufficiency, SAE recovery of approximately disentangled effect directions, principal-neuron alignment, and bounded transport/collider bias under post-treatment stratification. These assumptions are close to the desired conclusion and limit the force of the consistency theorem.

The evaluation is still narrow for a top-tier acceptance bar. The main quantitative benchmark uses only CelebA with two binary effects and ground-truth neurons selected by post hoc F1 alignment. It is unclear whether the method scales to more effects, correlated effects, continuous outcomes, weaker SAE monosemanticity, or domains unlike faces.

Baselines are relatively limited. The paper compares mostly against direct multiple testing and top-k selection, but not against stronger representation-level alternatives such as clustering of treatment-sensitive features, sparse regression/group testing, PCA/ICA-style residualization, causal feature learning variants, knockoff/selective-inference approaches, or other post-selection correction procedures.

The real-world experiment is intriguing but not fully convincing as evidence of scientific utility. It has very small sample size, drops Bonferroni correction, returns only two neurons, and relies mainly on qualitative interpretation plus one modest grooming F1 score. More quantitative validation with domain labels, held-out trials, or expert-blinded assessment would make the claim substantially stronger.

There is some tension between the statistical framing and the practical recommendation: the method identifies statistically significant representation shifts, but the authors acknowledge these may be artifacts and should not be used directly for treatment-effect estimation. This weakens the causal discovery claim unless the downstream validation workflow is formalized.

Reproducibility is only partial at submission time: the authors state that standalone code to reproduce all experiments will be released later. For a method whose behavior depends on SAE training choices and feature preprocessing, full scripts and seeds are important.

The writing is generally clear but contains several imprecisions and minor errors, and some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially phrases like first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and timely problem: exploratory causal effect discovery in randomized trials when outcomes are only indirectly observed through high-dimensional data such as images or videos.

The proposed Neural Effect Search procedure is conceptually appealing: recursively selecting a leading affected SAE code and then stratifying/residualizing on discovered codes is a plausible way to reduce redundant discoveries caused by entangled representations.

The manuscript provides a useful formal framing of the “significance collapse” issue: with increasing sample size or effect size, weakly entangled representation coordinates will eventually become statistically significant, making naive multiple testing hard to interpret.

The semi-synthetic CelebA experiments are fairly extensive, including ablations over sample size, effect size, encoder, SAE dimension, SAE nonlinearity, random seeds, residualization, treatment imbalance, zero-effect settings, and additional LASSO-style baselines.

The real-world ant-trial case study is compelling as a proof of concept: the method recovers a biologically meaningful grooming-related code as well as a background artifact related to experimental design, illustrating the potential value of exploratory discovery.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantee depends on very strong and largely untestable representation assumptions: foundation-model sufficiency, approximate SAE disentanglement, principal alignment of each effect with a unique coordinate, bounded leakage, and benign behavior under post-treatment stratification. These assumptions are close to requiring the desired solution structure rather than deriving it from realistic conditions.

The statistical validity of the adaptive recursive testing procedure is not fully convincing. Bonferroni correction is applied within each round, but the procedure adaptively selects variables and conditions on post-treatment codes in later rounds; the paper does not provide a satisfying finite-sample error-control argument for this adaptive pipeline.

The empirical validation is still narrow. The quantitative benchmark is semi-synthetic and built from CelebA attributes, where the ground-truth “affected neurons” are defined by best F1 alignment with known labels. This risks making evaluation depend heavily on the chosen SAE representation and may not reflect genuinely unknown scientific outcomes.

The real-world experiment is very small, with only 44 videos, and the authors explicitly disable Bonferroni correction there. As a result, the most scientifically interesting case study is mainly qualitative and does not strongly validate the claimed statistical procedure.

Baselines are incomplete. The comparisons are mostly against naive multiple testing, top-k selection, and simple LASSO variants. Stronger alternatives such as dimensionality reduction plus testing, sparse supervised/anti-causal feature selection with controlled FDR, clustering-based causal feature learning, knockoff-style selection, hierarchical testing, or representation-level two-sample tests are not adequately explored.

The paper’s core contribution is somewhat entangled with the current limitations of SAEs. The authors acknowledge that SAE identifiability and monosemanticity are not guaranteed, but the method’s usefulness depends critically on precisely these properties.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially statements that NES “disentangles” effects or identifies true affected outcome factors. The experiments show promising recovery of selected attribute-aligned codes under favorable conditions, but not robust causal outcome discovery in general.

Reproducibility is only partial: the appendix gives many details and a minimal snippet, but the paper does not appear to provide full code, trained SAE checkpoints, exact preprocessing, or enough implementation detail to easily reproduce the full pipeline end to end.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting problem: exploratory discovery of treatment-responsive outcomes from high-dimensional measurements in randomized trials, which is relevant to scientific ML and causal inference.

The distinction between hypothesis-driven causal analysis and exploratory effect discovery is clearly motivated, and the paper makes a reasonable attempt to connect foundation-model representations, sparse autoencoders, and multiple testing.
The semi-synthetic experiments include useful ablations over sample size, effect size, encoder choice, SAE dimension, residualization, and additional heuristic baselines.
weaknesses: The central causal claims rest on very strong and largely untestable representation assumptions: foundation-model sufficiency, SAE monosemanticity/principal alignment, and a stratification condition that effectively assumes away much of the difficult post-treatment conditioning problem.

The theoretical results are not very compelling. The “significance collapse” result is essentially the standard fact that any nonzero effect becomes significant with enough power, while the NES consistency proof depends on assumptions tailored to make recursive selection succeed.

The real-world evaluation is weak. The main ecological case has only 44 videos and disables Bonferroni correction due to low power, undermining the claimed statistically principled discovery procedure exactly where it matters most.

The real-data findings are not convincing as evidence of novel scientific discovery: one discovered code corresponds to a previously known grooming behavior, and the other is a background/batch artifact. Framing the artifact as a strength feels overstated.

The semi-synthetic benchmark is too narrow and favorable: ground-truth effects are tied to CelebA attributes for which the representation is explicitly checked to contain principal SAE neurons. This does not demonstrate robustness in realistic settings where concepts are continuous, distributed, ambiguous, or absent from the representation.

The baselines are mostly simple multiple-testing or selection heuristics. The paper does not adequately compare against stronger representation-level two-sample testing, sparse supervised probes with proper selection control, conditional randomization-style tests, or other high-dimensional outcome discovery methods.

The method conditions/stratifies on post-treatment learned codes, which can introduce collider and mediation-related biases. The paper acknowledges this but handles it via assumptions and bounded-error arguments rather than convincing diagnostics or empirical stress tests.

The paper repeatedly uses language such as “causal effect identification” and “statistically significant effects” in a way that risks overstating what is actually identified: significant differences in learned neural codes that may or may not map cleanly to scientific outcomes.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a top-tier submission: the paper provides many details and a snippet, but it is unclear whether complete code, trained SAEs, exact preprocessing, random seeds, and real-data annotations are released.

Overall, the contribution is interesting but not yet competitive for acceptance: the novelty is partly conceptual, the guarantees are assumption-heavy, and the empirical evidence does not adequately support the paper’s strongest claims.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: exploratory causal discovery of unknown outcomes in randomized experiments with high-dimensional unstructured measurements. The framing is compelling and connects causal inference, foundation-model representations, and sparse autoencoders in a clear way.

The central observation that standard multiple testing can become less interpretable as power increases, because many weakly entangled representation coordinates become significant, is insightful and well motivated. The synthetic illustration and semi-synthetic experiments make this failure mode easy to understand.

Neural Effect Search is a simple and appealing recursive procedure. The idea of selecting the strongest treatment-responsive code and then stratifying or residualizing subsequent tests against already discovered codes is intuitive and practically useful.

The empirical section is fairly extensive for a new method: the paper includes a semi-synthetic benchmark with known ground truth, ablations over sample size, effect size, encoder, SAE dimension, activation type, random seeds, propensity imbalance, no-effect settings, and additional LASSO-style baselines.

The real-world ant experiment is a strong qualitative proof of concept. Recovering both a known grooming-related effect and a background/design artifact demonstrates that the method can surface scientifically relevant signals as well as nuisance experimental biases.

The paper is candid about key limitations, especially the reliance on foundation-model sufficiency, SAE interpretability, and untestable representation assumptions. This improves the trustworthiness of the presentation.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees appear overstated. With fixed significance level alpha, Bonferroni controls false discoveries but does not make the probability of any null rejection vanish as n grows; claims such as exact convergence of the rejection set or halting with probability tending to one require alpha to shrink or additional assumptions. This affects both the paradox formalization and the NES consistency theorem.

The consistency result depends on very strong and largely untestable assumptions: linear effect decomposition in SAE space, full-rank effect directions, distinct principal neurons, margin conditions, and bounded bias from conditioning on post-treatment codes. These assumptions are plausible in the semi-synthetic setup but much less justified in real scientific data.

The recursive stratification/residualization conditions on variables affected by treatment, which can introduce post-treatment conditioning or collider bias. The paper discusses bounded bias, but the argument is not fully convincing as a general causal justification, and practical guidance for when NES is valid remains limited.

The real-world evaluation is promising but thin. It uses only one small trial, reports two discovered neurons, disables Bonferroni adjustment due to small sample size, and relies mainly on qualitative interpretation plus modest F1 scores for grooming/background prediction. This supports hypothesis generation more than validated causal discovery.

There is a potential independence issue in the ant experiment: the paper mentions n=44 videos but trains/tests on frame-level codes. If statistical tests are effectively using many correlated frames without video-level clustering or aggregation, p-values and significance claims may be anti-conservative.

The semi-synthetic benchmark is useful but narrow: the true effects are CelebA attributes deliberately chosen to be well represented by the foundation model/SAE, and the ground-truth affected neurons are defined by the same representation via best F1. This may favor methods like NES and does not fully test cases where effects are distributed, continuous, nonlinear, or poorly captured by a single SAE code.

Baselines are reasonable but not exhaustive. Comparisons to alternative representation-level discovery methods, conditional randomization/permutation procedures, clustering-based causal feature learning variants, hierarchical testing, knockoffs, or post-selection inference would strengthen the empirical case.

The paper sometimes uses language suggesting causal effect identification, while the practical output is better described as statistically significant treatment-associated representation features requiring expert interpretation and follow-up labeling. The authors acknowledge this, but some main claims remain stronger than the evidence.
